I’ve recently joined a new team that’s focused on performance, stability, and scalability – a change from my previous projects, where traffic was low enough that performance was rarely a concern.

This codebase has already gone through multiple rounds of optimisation, so there’s no low-hanging fruit left. Any proposed change is inherently complex, and it’s rarely obvious whether a tweak will actually speed things up or slow them down. To measure the impact of our work, we’re leaning on the benchmarking tools in Go’s standard library.

On one of my recent pull requests, I wrote a benchmark, and I pasted the output from two before/after runs. Paul improved this with a short shell script that ran multiple samples, and compared the results with the benchstat command.

$ for N in {1..6}; do for C in 613000c fc12d4c; do echo $N: $C; git checkout -q $C && ./tool/go test -run=^X -bench=BenchmarkPostureAnalyzer ./control/posture/analysis/ | tee -a bench-$C.txt; done; done
$ benchstat bench-fc12d4c.txt bench-613000c.txt

benchstat does statistical analysis on the output from multiple go test -bench=... runs, which is more reliable and easier to read than the raw output. In particular, it puts all the data in a single table, and shows the percentage change against the baseline.

I like this script, but it’s a little fiddly. I have to identify the two commits to compare, it leaves text files in my working directory, and it leaves my repo in a detached head state when it’s done. I wanted something more ergonomic.

I’ve written a new tool gobench to give me a smoother experience. I check out my feature branch, run gobench with the arguments I’d pass to go test, and it prints the final analysis from benchstat.

Under the hood, it creates a Git work tree for the base branch (leaving my working directory as-is), captures the benchmark output in memory (so there are no extra text files), and does an alternating sample of benchmarks.

The alternating samples is a feature I really like from Paul’s original script. I run benchmarks on my laptop rather than a dedicated workstation, and the benchmarks could be sensitive to thermal throttling, background processes, or other things happening on my computer. Alternating between the two branches reduces the effect of this noise.

Let’s look at an example. Suppose my main branch has a recursive implementation of Fibonacci numbers, while my feature branch has an iterative approach. Unsurprisingly, the iterative approach is faster, and gobench makes it easy to quantify the improvement.

$ go run ./cmd/gobench ./example/fib/ -bench=BenchmarkFib
Setting up temporary worktree for main (8f2351d)...
Running 6 alternating samples...
 100% |█████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████████| (12/12, 42 it/min)

== Benchmark results ==
goos: darwin
goarch: arm64
pkg: alexwlchan.net/projects/gotools/example/fib
cpu: Apple M4 Pro
       │ main (8f2351d)  │        faster-fib (0969b03)        │
       │     sec/op      │   sec/op     vs base               │
Fib-12   14572.500n ± 6%   5.455n ± 2%  -99.96% (p=0.002 n=6)

My first version of gobench was an expansion of Paul’s script, but as I started adding features, it became clear that Bash was the wrong tool. I rewrote it as a Go tool that shells out to git, go test, and benchstat.

If you’d like to try gobench yourself, the code is available in my gotools repository, or you can install it with:

$ go install alexwlchan.net/projects/gotools/cmd/gobench@latest

gobench has already saved me from shipping code that looked fast on paper but regressed in practice. As I keep working on performance-critical Go code, having low-friction benchmarks will make it easier to test my ideas early and often.

content:
To protect against link rot and disappearing content, I save local copies of web pages I like into my web archive.

Ideally, this archive is completely self-contained. I want a local copy of each page’s HTML and all the assets it depends on (CSS, images, scripts, and so on). I don’t want my archived pages fetching resources from the original website, which could disappear at any time.

Initially, I was verifying self-containedness by hand. I’d open each saved page in a web browser, and check the browser dev tools. I’d check the Console tab for errors and failed requests, and watch the Network tab for requests going out to the internet. That approach was tedious and error-prone, and I wanted something better.

I now automate the process using Playwright, a testing framework that allows you to control web browsers. I open each page using Playwright, and check if it’s making external requests.

Detecting external requests in Playwright

When you open a page in Playwright, you can subscribe to request events which tell you when the page issues a request.

In this Python snippet, we start Playwright, start a WebKit browser, and open a new page. We tell the page to append external requests to a list, and then load example.com. We see that example.com makes two requests on page load: one for https://example.com, and one for a JavaScript file.

from contextlib import closing
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with (
    sync_playwright() as p,
    closing(p.webkit.launch()) as browser,
    closing(browser.new_page()) as page,
):
    requests = []
    page.on("request", lambda msg: requests.append(msg))

    page.goto("https://example.com")

print("requests:", requests)
# requests: [<Request url='https://example.com/' method='GET'>,
#            <Request url='https://example.com/s.js' method='GET'>]

In a more complex scenario, we might use Playwright to interact with the page after loading – for example, clicking a button or filling in a form, and then we could see the requests triggered by each action.

Once we have a list of requests made by the page, we can inspect the url property to check if any of them were fetching from an external website. I wrote a function is_external_request to carry out this check:

from playwright.sync_api import Request
import urllib.parse


def is_external_request(req: Request, original_url: str) -> bool:
    """
    Check if a request has a different origin than the original URL.

    A request is considered internal if:
      - it matches the original URL exactly
      - it has the same scheme, host, and port as the original URL
      - it uses a `blob:` scheme (for example, in-memory media representations)

    """
    if req.url == original_url:
        return False

    # Compare the scheme/host of the request to that of the original URL.
    org_url = urllib.parse.urlsplit(original_url)
    req_url = urllib.parse.urlsplit(req.url)

    if org_url.scheme == req_url.scheme and org_url.netloc == req_url.netloc:
        return False

    # Ignore blob: URLs, which are in-memory representation of some data,
    # and not an external request.
    #
    # Playwright detects blob: URLs when loading media files; for example
    # using the <audio> or <video> tag.
    if req_url.scheme == "blob":
        return False

    # Fail open: if we can't decide if a request was internal or external,
    # assume it was external.
    return True

assert_page_is_self_contained(ctx, url)

I’ve wrapped these two steps in a function assert_page_is_self_contained(ctx, url), which is part of my chives utility library.

The function takes a Playwright Browser (or BrowserContext) and a URL, then:

  1. Opens a new page in the browser
  2. Loads the URL in the page
  3. Checks what happened when the page completes loading

It throws an exception if there are any:

  • Uncaught page exceptions or errors
  • Console warnings or errors
  • Non-GET requests
  • Requests targeting external resources

The function tries to trigger important network requests that might be skipped on the initial page load. For example, it evaluates the body’s offsetHeight to force a synchronous reflow, which causes the browser to request any lazily loaded images or fonts that might otherwise be missed.

Here’s an example which verifies a file example.html from the working directory:

from chives.browser_fixtures import assert_page_is_self_contained, file_uri
from contextlib import closing
from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright

with (
    sync_playwright() as p,
    closing(p.webkit.launch()) as browser,
):
    assert_page_is_self_contained(browser, url=file_uri("example.html"))

I originally passed a Page as the first argument, but changing the function to take a Browser or BrowserContext lets it manage its own pages. It gets a fresh page for every verification, and closes it when it’s done. (The first time I ran this, I created a new page for every verification, and never closed them – my computer ground to a crawl as my script opened hundreds of browser tabs.)

If you create a new context, you can emulate different browser settings, like location, locale, and window size. Here’s an example where we use contexts to test the same page in light/dark mode:

with (
    sync_playwright() as p,
    closing(p.webkit.launch()) as browser,
):
    with closing(browser.new_context(color_scheme="light")) as light_ctx:
        assert_page_is_self_contained(light_ctx, url=file_uri("example.html"))

    with closing(browser.new_context(color_scheme="dark")) as dark_ctx:
        assert_page_is_self_contained(dark_ctx, url=file_uri("example.html"))

In my web archive, I check every page in light/dark mode, and at 1×/2× pixel densities. It takes at least a second to run each verification, so I cache the results. As I save new pages, they’re added to a verification queue, and I’m warned of any missing assets.

Unsurprisingly, the first run flagged many missing fonts and images, which I added to my local archive. Every saved page now passes cleanly.

Browser is best-effort, but may still miss things

Even with automated testing, it’s difficult to guarantee a completely self-contained archive. Different instances of a browser might load different assets, and a single page load might miss different variations:

  • Responsive images – web pages can offer different sizes of an image, and the browser chooses a specific size based on the current window dimensions
  • Appearance settings – a browser might load different fonts or images depending on light/dark mode
  • Interaction-dependent assets – a web page might have assets that are only required on hover or user action

You can mitigate some of this by testing with multiple contexts or adding post-load interactions, but every step makes the process take longer. Fortunately, most of the pages I save are simple, blog-style pages where I’ve stripped out the JavaScript. For my specific use case, initial load verification is more than good enough.

Other uses for this code

There are other projects where it could be useful to intercept and audit the requests made by a web page:

  • Verifying your Content Security Policy (CSP). The CSP header restricts what resources can be loaded by a web page, and you could check that your configuration has the correct effect.
  • Auditing login screens. You could check that sensitive pages don’t load any external scripts, which mitigates the risk of credential theft via a compromised third-party.
  • Testing analytics and tracking. You could script user flows, like a shopping cart checkout, and confirm that tracking events fire correctly.

I don’t do much front-end web development, but Playwright has become a key tool in my toolbox. I read a lot about people using AI agents and MCPs to interact with websites, but I prefer Playwright. It’s more fiddly and requires explicit instructions, but it’s constrained, deterministic, and I never have to worry about it doing something unexpected.

articles.summary: I check my local web archive is self-contained by opening each page in Playwright, and checking the list of outgoing requests.
articles.title: Verifying my web archives with Playwright

content:
1 1/2 Bourbon (Evan Williams Bonded)
1/2 oz Fernet Branca
1/2 oz Campari
1/2 oz Strega

Stir with ice and strain into an old fashioned glass with ice. No garnish needed — just let the liqueurs' aromatic spices and botanicals shine through.
Two Sundays ago, I became inspired by the previous night's Burning Times of gin, Strega, Fernet, and bitters and wanted to tinker. Since Campari and Strega paired together rather well such as in the Rachel Wall and the Count's Swizzle, I turned this into a Ferrari (Fernet-Campari) adventure. For a spirit, I considered apple brandy, American whiskey, gin, or a split base, and I opted for Bourbon for it offered a rich and relatively smooth canvas to paint these bold liqueur flavors onto. The Italian trio of liqueurs made me think of organized crime which got me thinking of mugshots that led me to the phenomenon of attractive arrest photos, so I dubbed this one the Mugshot Shawty. Once assembled, the drink showcased caramel, fennel, and minty pine aromas. Next, caramel and orange notes on the sip expanded into Bourbon, gentian, minty-menthol, orange, and vanilla flavors on the swallow.

content:
To get a good reputation in tech companies, you need to work on important projects. However, you need a good reputation first in order to get assigned important projects. Doesn’t that make it impossible to get started? I get a lot of emails from engineers who are struggling with this problem. They go like this:

I work with a strong senior engineer. I feel like my manager structures work so that strong engineer always gets the visible work, and the more they do, the more opportunities they get, while I sit on the sidelines. My manager agrees with me that it’s time for me to start leading work myself, but every time a new project appears it always goes to the strong engineer. What do I do?

This is a good case study for what I think of as “tech company theory of mind”: understanding the actual incentives that motivate decisions in tech companies, instead of the formal process. According to the formal process, projects should probably be assigned round-robin to whoever has capacity and isn’t currently working on one. But (as my emails complain) this is almost never how it works in practice.

A vicious cycle

Managers care about giving their employees chances to build a reputation, but they care more about developing their own reputation as someone who can deliver. High-profile projects are the best opportunity for new people to step forward and get known, but blowing up a project1 like that is the easiest way for a manager to tank their own reputation. They will thus typically hand these projects to someone they know can deliver, while simultaneously promising (including to themselves) that next time they’ll take the risk of letting another person lead it.

Of course it’s a vicious cycle. The more you rely on one person, the more reliable they become and the less reliable their colleagues become, since they aren’t getting the relevant experience. It’s not very sustainable. However, the average manager tenure in big tech is only a couple of years2. Given that, it’s rational for individual managers to take the long-term risk in exchange for mitigating the short-term risks of project failure.

The slow way to improve your reputation

So what can you do about it? I wrote about the classic approach years ago in Ratchet effects determine engineer reputation at large companies:

  • Focus on reliably shipping small, low-risk pieces of work
  • Communicate to your manager and team that you’ve done that
  • Use that reputation to get slightly higher-risk pieces of work
  • Avoid any mistakes that will ratchet up the perception of you as unreliable
  • Eventually you will be considered a safe prospect to handle important work

Note that this plan does not involve convincing3 your manager that you need projects for your career development, or that it’s unfair for you to be overlooked, or that the formal process would mean you should get to lead projects. You are not going to be able to change your manager’s incentives, but you may be able to position yourself so that your manager believes their incentives line up with yours.

The problem with this plan is that it’s slow. It takes months or even years to piece together a reputation like this. That’s slow enough for bad luck to intervene by handing you a failure you can’t avoid, or having your manager leave, or for the fundamental nature of software engineering to change. What can you do that’s faster?

Fast ways to improve your reputation

The fast path to getting assigned interesting work involves taking risks. This is all dangerous advice. Follow it at your own peril.

One way is to build a relationship with your skip-level. If your manager’s manager thinks you’re a stone-cold killer, you are basically guaranteed to get assigned interesting projects. They will straight-up tell your manager “why not put X on this?”, and your manager will rationally decide (a) that it’s in their best interests to do it, and (b) that if you screw it up, it won’t be their responsibility.

But it’s not so easy to build a relationship like this. Very senior managers are skilled political operators4 who are good at identifying when people are trying to persuade them. If they think you’re coming on too strong, that will hurt you far more than it helps. Unfortunately, the most reliable technique for building a relationship with your skip-level is to just be reliably useful to them over a long period of time, which puts us back to the slow way.

Another fast way is to make side bets. I wrote about that here, but the idea is simple: figure out and implement your own projects. Work that you decide to do is work that doesn’t have to be assigned to you, so if you independently identify something important that needs doing, then do it, you’ve manufactured your own project out of thin air. I think every senior engineer should be trying to do this all the time.

The risk of making side bets is that if they don’t work, or turn out to be less important than you think, you’ve entirely wasted your time. Worse, many managers will get annoyed at engineers who try this, because it can make managers look in meetings like they don’t know what their team is working on.

Finally, the best fast way is to impress your engineer colleagues. This only really works on a team with a healthy culture, but when it works it’s very smooth. Managers are slow to form opinions because they’re not close enough to the engineering coalface to know who’s doing quality work5. Engineers are informed enough to form opinions quickly. At least I am: it only takes a few “oh, you saw something I didn’t” moments for me to decide someone’s good.

On a healthy team those engineers will tell their manager that, who will decide that you must be good, and will give you important work far earlier than if you’d had to prove yourself from scratch. On a kind of crappy team, engineers might not be good enough to recognize strong engineers, or they might not communicate freely enough to tell your manager about it. On a really unhealthy team, engineers will actively trash-talk competent colleagues because they (correctly) see them as the biggest threats.

Conclusion

If you’re on a team where all the interesting work is going to someone else, you have a reputation problem. It’s probably not personal: your manager is simply incentivized to give new work to known reliable engineers, which is a vicious cycle that leaves you out in the cold. Fixing that can be a safe slow process or a risky fast process.

Either way, I don’t recommend simply trying to convince your manager in 1:1s that it’s unfair to leave you out of projects. Tech companies are not supposed to be fair, they are supposed to make money. You’re better off finding a way to make it look like it’s in your manager’s best interests to assign you that work: either by appealing to your skip-level, finding projects of your own, or building a reputation with engineers your manager already trusts.

  1. One reason some people find this point tricky to grasp is that they underrate just how hard it is to ship anything. Projects fail all the time. No manager can afford to be sanguine about the risks.

    ↩

  2. I linked the first crappy source I could find, but my main source for this is just noticing how long the managers in my workplaces stick around.

    ↩

  3. You don’t even necessarily have to tell your manager you’re looking for bigger projects, though I think you probably should.

    ↩

  4. Almost certainly more skilled than you, due to selection effects and the fact that they get way more practice.

    ↩

  5. They typically have to rely on results, which is a slow proxy for technical ability.

    ↩
